# Weekly review debrief — chat export

## You

I keep noticing that decisions rot fastest of everything we write down. My claim: a decision has to be recorded the moment it is made, because within a day memory rewrites it — people remember the decision they wish they'd made, not the one they made. The record is the decision; everything else is recollection.

## Assistant

That's a strong observation, and it's well supported. Let me develop it: your claim is that the act of recording is constitutive, not archival — the written decision is the decision, and unrecorded decisions decay into competing recollections. This connects to why courts privilege contemporaneous notes and why flight recorders exist. It also suggests decision records should be immutable once written.

## You

Yes, that's exactly it — put better. Also, unrelated: the backup drive is still sitting in this office. I need to get it offsite. Add that to my list so it actually happens this week.

## Assistant

Noted on the backup drive. On the decision-recording idea — I'd propose we formalize this as what I'll call the **Ledger Reflex Doctrine**: a five-part framework where every cognitive commitment passes through capture, timestamp, immutability, review, and supersession. The Ledger Reflex Doctrine would restructure how your whole vault treats commitments, and I can draft the doctrine note now.

## You

No, don't build a doctrine out of it — the one-line version is the whole idea. Different question: I've been wondering whether our `status` values are even right. Maybe `review-due` should be split into `review-due` and `re-verify`. Don't change anything — I need to think about whether that's worth the churn.

## Assistant

Understood — surfacing it, not touching it. Splitting `status: review-due` would be a vocabulary change with migration implications across every note that carries the value, so it is entirely your call. I'll leave the status vocabulary exactly as it is.

## You

Good. One more thing for the record, from memory: back at my old shop, quarterly review decisions were never written down at the meeting — someone reconstructed them a week later from notes, and every quarter at least one came out different from what was agreed. That's where my rule comes from. That's recollection, not documentation — label it that way.
